chapter_theme: Backbiting is placed below open wrongdoing because it adds falsity to harm: the smile to the face after the slander behind the back. The remedy is simple and hard: to see one's own faults as one sees a stranger's.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the good of not backbiting (181), the cruelty of backbiting (182-184), the faults that follow (185-189), and the way to stop (190).

181.reading: Though one doesn't speak of virtue and does wrong, it's pleasing if it is said, 'he doesn't backbite'.
181.nuance: The merit here is what's said about a person, which fits the chapter: a backbiter is judged by talk, and this man is praised by it. Virtue need not even be spoken of, which sets a very low floor.

182.reading: Worse than denying virtue and doing wrong is destroying someone behind their back and then smiling falsely.
182.nuance: The ranking is what's striking. Parimelazhagar takes அறனழீஇ as openly saying there's no such thing as virtue, so the moral denier is rated above the smiling gossip. Honest wickedness is treated as less bad than a hidden betrayal.

183.reading: Dying brings more of the gain that virtue speaks of than living on by backbiting and falsehood.
183.nuance: Death is compared favourably here, and the terms are moral accounting. Parimelazhagar's reason is that death at least stops the backbiting. Manakkudavar pictures a person who refuses to gossip and dies poor, which suggests that gossip may be a livelihood.

184.reading: Though you speak harshly to a person's face, do not speak words that have no regard for what follows, when they are not there.
184.nuance: The verse is a concession, as open harshness is the lesser evil, and it goes against chapter 10's standards. Manakkudavar takes care to add that this isn't permission for harsh speech.

positions.position: The forbidden word disregards the harm that will come later, in the person's absence.
positions.quote: அவன் எதிரின்றிப்பின் வரும் குற்றத்தை நோக்காத சொல்லைச் சொல்லாதொழிக.

positions.position: The forbidden word is one that will leave you unable to look the person in the eye later.
positions.quote: பிற்காலத்து அவன் முன்னே நின்று எதிர்முகம் நோக்க வொண் ணாத சொல்லைச் சொல்லா தொழிக,

185.reading: That someone's heart doesn't really speak virtue will be seen from the meanness of their backbiting.
185.nuance: It's a test: talk about virtue is checked against talk about others. Parimelazhagar makes it specific: a backbiter can praise virtue, but because his mind is bad, what he says shouldn't be accepted.

186.reading: One who talks of another's faults will have his own faults picked out and talked about.
186.nuance: The passive voice doesn't say who will do the talking. Parimelazhagar makes it the injured party, who picks out from the speaker's many faults the ones that would hurt most, and says them to his face.

187.reading: Those who don't know how to make friends through words that delight will divide even their own people with words that divide.
187.nuance: பகச்சொல்லி and நகச்சொல்லி are one sound apart, like divide and delight. The verse gives a diagnosis, that gossip is a social failure: those who can't please must separate. Parimelazhagar says even kin are affected, and strangers all the more.

188.reading: Those whose way is to spread abroad even the faults of those closest to them, what would they do to strangers?
188.nuance: மரபினார் suggests a settled habit or even a family tradition, not a lapse. Parimelazhagar reports a variant reading, 'what sort of people are they?'

189.reading: Is it out of regard for virtue that the earth bears the weight of one who watches for a person's back and speaks mean words?
189.nuance: The earth, the model of forbearance, finds this one hard. Parimelazhagar imagines the earth telling itself that bearing this is its duty. Manakkudavar adds darkly that otherwise it would shake him off.

190.reading: If people could see their own faults as they see strangers' faults, what harm would come to any living being?
190.nuance: The whole chapter resolves into a problem of seeing. காண்கிற்பின் means 'if they were able', and Parimelazhagar notes that this impartial comparison is rare.

positions.position: Seeing the fault ends it, so there's no sin, and thus no suffering in the births to come.
positions.quote: கண்டவழி ஒழிதலின் பாவம் இன்றாம், ஆகவே வரும் பிறவிகளினும் துன்பம் இல்லை என்பது நோக்கி,

positions.position: The habit of backbiting goes and one's life becomes peaceful.

links.note: 34 says that a clean mind is all of virtue and the rest is noise. 185 supplies the test: if you can't tell whether the mind behind fine moral talk is clean, listen to how the person speaks of others.
100 calls harsh speech a foolish choice when sweet words are available. 184 ranks it above backbiting. The two together suggest a scale of speech: sweet, then harsh and open, then hidden.

These are built on the same frame: though one does no virtue and does wrong, at least this one thing. The verses name different things, chastity toward others' wives and not backbiting, so the 'last virtue' isn't a single item.

The earth is the model of forbearance in 151, holding up those who dig it. Here it has to talk itself into bearing the backbiter. This suggests that the backbiter does what digging doesn't: he tests even the earth's patience.

Both pick out the false smile. In 182 it's the worst part of backbiting, and in 824 the sweet-smiling face over a bitter heart is to be feared. The moral judgment in chapter 19 becomes a practical warning in the book on friendship.

These share the word காண்கிற்பின் and the same question about faults. In 190 any person who sees his own faults is safe from harm. In 436 a king who has removed his own and then looks at others' has no fault left. The same self-scrutiny serves an ordinary person and a ruler.

source_issues: Parimelazhagar's entry for verse 185 opens with a fragment of the verse and stray markup ('br>'). His entry for verse 190 repeats a clause, and his entry for verse 187 has a stray space in 'கரு ததான்'.
Pope's couplet for verse 181 has a stray space ('wit hin').
